Copper catalysis for highly selective aerobic
oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes/ketones†
Di Zhaia and Shengming Ma *a,b
Oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes/ketones is a transformation of fundamental importance. Usually stoi-
chiometric amounts of oxidants are required for these types of reactions. Although aerobic oxidations
have been studied, there exist challenges: complicated additives, toxic or expensive catalyst(s), a large
amount of base or molecular sieves, limited substrate scope, isomerization of CvC bonds, . Herein,
a general and practical room temperature aerobic oxidation of different types of alcohols including alle-
nols, alkenols, propargylic alcohols, benzylic alcohols, and aliphatic alcohols in MeCN (acetonitrile) or
DCE (1,2-dichloroethane) using readily available and cheap
\mathsf { C u } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } { \cdot } 3 \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { O }
and TEMPO (2,2,6,6-tetra-
methyl-1-piperidinyloxy) or 4-HO-TEMPO as the catalysts forming aldehydes or ketones with an excellent
selectivity has been developed. Some thirty to forty mmol scale reactions have been demonstrated.
Introduction
Aldehydes and ketones are very common and useful chemicals
for organic chemistry, cosmetics, medicinal chemistry, and
materials science. They are usually synthesized via oxidation of
alcohols both in academic laboratories and industries.
Traditional protocols for the oxidation of alcohols require at
least a stoichiometric amount of certain expensive oxidants
such as MnO2, CrO3, PCC, PDC, IBX, etc., which would yield
an equal amount of waste, resulting in a serious problem for
isolation of the products and a big burden to the environ-
ment.1 Therefore, much attention has been focused on the
eco-friendly aerobic oxidation of alcohols.1,2
In 1981, Gilbride and his coworkers3a found that there is a
high level of copper in the recovered product of the protein
from the serum of a horseshoe crab. Later, Linzen and his
coworkers3b found in the hemocyanins of arthropods and
mollusks two copper atoms bound directly to side chains at
the site of oxygen binding while a single iron was contained in
the heme of hemoglobin. Thus, copper is the metal of choice
in nature to carry oxygen. In fact, Semmelhack, Stahl,
Iwabuchi, Markó, and their coworkers4–6 have made very
important contributions in the area of using copper as the
catalyst for aerobic oxidation of alcohols. In addition, a cata-
lytic amount each of Cu(MeCN) PF , DBED, and
\mathrm { D M A P } ^ { \mathrm { 7 } }
or
CuCl combined with highly toxic
\mathrm { O s O _ { 4 } } ^ { 8 }
may also catalyze this
reaction, however, a large amount of 4 Å molecular sieves was
required, which makes the reaction non-practical in large-scale
productions (Scheme 1). Complicated additives, toxic or expen-
sive catalyst(s), high temperature, a large amount of base or
molecular sieves, limited substrate scope (for further
examples, see also: Tables 3 and 4), serious isomerization of
Z CvC bonds,5c etc. call for the development of new catalytic
recipes. Thus, cost-effective highly selective aerobic oxidation
of alcohols with a wide scope and academic/industrial poten-
tial at room temperature is of high current interest. The
common approach is usually the development of ligands or
more expensive copper catalysts with more complicated amine
N-oxyls.4,5 We tried the copper anion effect and observed that
these above-mentioned challenges may be addressed by apply-
ing copper nitrate and TEMPO as catalysts, oxidizing a very
wide scope of alcohols to aldehydes or ketones with an excel-
lent selectivity (Scheme 1).
Results and discussion
At the beginning of our study, we selected 1-phenyl-2-heptyn-1-
ol 1a as the model starting material to optimize the reaction
conditions of the copper-catalyzed aerobic oxidation reaction.
First, different solvents were screened; when NMP, cyclohexane
and MeNO were used as solvents (Table 1, entries 1, 2 and 4),
56–84% of 1a was recovered. Ethers such as dioxane, THF, and
Et2O only gave 42–85% yield of 2a (Table 1, entries 3, 5, and 6).
DCM and toluene were also examined with 91% and 92% yield

Control experiments disclosed the importance of

and TEMPO for this transformation (Table 2, entries 7 and 8).
Control experiments show that terminal propargylic
alcohol, 1-(4-methylphenyl)-2-propyn-1-ol 1b, could not be
transformed into the corresponding ketone 2b by the most
popular copper catalytic systems,4f,5a,b most probably due to
the basic nature of the reaction conditions (Table 3,
entries 1–3). The current method could afford 1-(4-methyl-
phenyl)-2-propyn-1-one 2b in 94% NMR yield (Table
entry 6). Since terminal alkynones are a type of very useful
compounds in organic synthesis, we demonstrated the scope
carefully. Besides 4-methylphenyl, other electron-withdrawing
and electron-donating group substituted phenyl groups,
thienyl and even
n { \mathrm { - C } } _ { 9 } \mathrm { H } _ { 1 9 }
substituted terminal propargylic
alcohols provided the desired alkynones 2b–2h in good to
excellent yields (Table 4, entries 1–7).
We also demonstrated the scope of the oxidation reaction
of non-terminal propargylic alcohols to the corresponding
aldehydes or ketones. When
\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }
is Ph, different groups including
n-Bu, cyclopropyl, Ph and TMS may be introduced as the
\mathbb { R } ^ { 1 }
group with excellent yields (Table
entries 1–4, 2a and 2i–2k).

may also be n-Bu with
\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }
being different electron-withdraw-
ing and electron-donating group substituted phenyl groups,

is aryl and
\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }
is

yields (Table
entries 14–17, 2u–2x). The tolerance of syntheti-

ing the potential of this methodology (Tables 4 and 5).

bond is very limited for both primary alcohols and secondary

Conclusions
In conclusion, we have developed an eco-friendly and practical
efficient aerobic oxidation of different alcohols to aldehydes/
ketones using
\mathrm { C u } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } { \cdot } 3 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }
and TEMPO as catalysts. This
protocol tolerates most common alcohols in organic synthesis
such as propargylic alcohols, allylic alcohols, allenols, benzylic
alcohols and normal alkanols, providing the corresponding
aldehydes/ketones in good to excellent yields with an excellent
selectivity. The oxidation reaction may be easily executed on a
practical scale in an academic laboratory and no over-oxidation
has been observed. Further studies of this copper catalytic
system including the application in industrial scale pro-
ductions are being actively pursued by our group.
